Q: How to split a column into 2 headings and fill with data from another column in R A:

This is indeed a "normal" reshape wider / pivot_wider operation. Only the column name requirement makes it just a tad special. Use names_glue to combine your PLANE names with the COORDINATE name from your values, e.g.

library(tidyr)
pivot_wider(data, 
   names_from = PLANE, 
   values_from = COORDINATE, 
   names_glue = "{PLANE}{.value}")

Q: How can I speed up vertices showing and animation? A:

First of all, pygame.key.get_pressed()[pygame.K_RIGHT] and pygame.key.get_pressed()[pygame.K_LEFT] are recomputed len(vertices) times while this is not actually needed. While you can pre-compute it before the loop, the value should not even change inside the loop so you should write multiple specialised loops. Besides, the for i in range(...): structure is more idiomatic and certainly a bit faster. Moreover, project(vertices[i]) is computed twice. You can compute it only once. Be aware that the standard Python implementation (the CPython interpreter) optimise nearly nothing (as opposed to compilers). Something like that should be faster:

for i in range(len(vertices)):
    vertices[i] = animate(i)

if pygame.key.get_pressed()[pygame.K_RIGHT]: # Only evaluated once per frame
    rotVec = [0, 2*dt, 0]
    for i in range(len(vertices)):
        vertices[i] = rotate_3d(vertices[i], rotVec)

if pygame.key.get_pressed()[pygame.K_LEFT]: # Only evaluated once per frame
    rotVec = [0, -2*dt, 0]
    for i in range(len(vertices)):
        vertices[i] = rotate_3d(vertices[i], rotVec)

for i in range(len(vertices)):
    projected = project(vertices[i]) # Only evaluated once per iteration
    pygame.draw.circle(screen, [0,160,20], projected, 2)
    text = font.render(str(i), False, [255,255,255])
    screen.blit(text, projected)

pygame.display.flip()
time.sleep(dt)
screen.fill([0,0,0])

This should be still quite slow compared to the optimal implementation. The key to make this faster is to use Numpy. This should be at least an order of magnitude faster. That being said, this means:

  • vertices should be a Numpy array;
  • animate must now operate on a Numpy arrays (at least internally);
  • same for rotate_3d: this is basically a matrix multiplication (with a precomputed rotation matrix) that can be done with A @ B in Numpy;
  • same for project which can also be implemented with a matrix multiplication;
  • use a loop iterating on Numpy items (and convert the array to a list for sake of performance just before with youArray.tolist()) for the last PyGame-related operations.

If the later is too slow, then I advise you to use OpenGL instead of PyGame (lower level but also more complicated for beginners). OpenGL can operate directly on Numpy array so there is no list conversions (Python lists are inherently slow). If this is still slow, the fastest solution is probably to write a shader for the circles, but this is certainly complicated for a beginner. Text rendering is known to be quite expensive (especially high-quality one).

Q: What is the different of <div> and <span> display : block; A:

In the early days of HTML, the <div> tag did not exist. It was made by Microsoft to work exclusively with Internet Explorer (free on any PCs) and with the aim of kill other browsers (Erwise, Mosaic, Netscape, Web Explorer, Arena, etc.) that adhered to the HTML-1 standard (with the <layer> tag rejected by IE).

see also : https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Div_and_span

Q: How can an embedded database support PostgreSQL syntax without running a PostgreSQL server? A:

What are the common approaches used by embedded databases to support PostgreSQL-compatible syntax?

The common approach is to run PostgreSQL. For example Zonky Embedded PostgreSQL uses standard PostgreSQL binaries, it just runs a short-lived instance from the client instead of configuring a daemon service.

This is a fork of OpenTable Embedded PostgreSQL which now runs PostgreSQL in a Docker container.

Are there open-source projects or references for implementing a PostgreSQL-like query planner in a lightweight engine?

There are packages to implement a PostgreSQL-compatible query parser, for example pganalyze/libpg_query.

Implementing a whole query engine to execute queries is a different task. You have to implement storage, concurrency, security, and so on. If you intend pglite to be embedded, at least you don't have to implement networking.

Is it realistic to support a meaningful subset of PostgreSQL features without implementing the full PostgreSQL architecture?

If you are the only user of pglite, then you can implement the subset of features you will need in your project.

But if you expect other people to use pglite, very soon you will get requests for features of PostgreSQL you didn't think were important, but are needed for their project.

For example, do you intend to implement user-defined functions, triggers, procedures, and rules? If not, how will you respond to users who say they want to use pglite to test their application, but they have developed hundreds of such stored routines?

How about system catalogs and system views?

How about the hundreds of builtin functions of PostgreSQL? Not just for JSON, but array functions, set returning functions, system information...

How about the many popular extensions to PostgreSQL, like PostGIS, pgcrypto, pg_stat_statements, pgvector, tablefunc, and many others.

Another thing you need to decide is which version of PostgreSQL does pglite support? New features are added in each version, as well as more subtle changes to the behavior of, for instance, the query planner.

If your embedded solution emulates PostgreSQL syntax and behavior, you will have to track the PostgreSQL project continually and update your pglite project to match. Alternatively, declare that pglite is compatible only with PostgreSQL 18.1 and leave that fixed for all time.
